migrationNotes: Spine: a bath tap that opens wider every minute is counted two ways, by the area under its rate graph and by a running total that is an antiderivative, and the agreement gives end-value subtraction, then why the constant cancels, then why the running total grows at the current rate.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): cal-the-two-ideas-connect-1 (integral of 2x from 1 to 3) and -10 (integral of 4x with F = 2x²). The teaching screens, the worked example and the faded example cover them.
Prompts rewritten to stand alone: -7 (was the opener's question).

lesson.title: Rates and areas connect

lead.text: Start with the bath from the opener. After t minutes the tap delivers 2t litres per minute, so at 1 minute it delivers 2 litres per minute and at 2 minutes it delivers 4. Draw that rate against time and you get a straight line rising from the origin. The area under the line is the water that has flowed in.

Take the first two minutes. The area under the line is a triangle with a base of 2 minutes and a height of 4 litres per minute, so it is ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 litres. The units agree with this: minutes multiplied by litres per minute leave litres.

afterFigure.text: The first minute alone gives a triangle with a base of 1 and a height of 2, so its area is ½ × 1 × 2 = 1 litre. Triangles work here because the rate is a straight line from zero. Most rates have no such tidy shape, and a method that only handles neat shapes will not carry us far. The next screens look for one that does.

lead.text: Use the same triangle method on the first three minutes of the tap.

reveal.text: You found 9 litres from a triangle. That is more than the 4 litres of the first two minutes, because the tap keeps opening. The next screen reaches this 9 a second way.

lead.text: Now count the same water another way. Instead of finding one area at a time, keep a running total. Let A(x) be the litres that have run in by minute x. The triangles give A(1) = 1 and A(2) = 4, and the last screen gave A(3) = 9.
Each total is the square of its minute. The triangle up to minute x has a base of x and a height of 2x, so its area is ½ × x × 2x = x². The running total is A(x) = x².

afterFigure.text: Compare that with the lesson on undoing derivatives. The derivative of x² is 2x, which is the tap's rate, so x² is an antiderivative of 2x. This is no coincidence. The rate says how fast the water is arriving at each moment, so the slope of the running total has to equal the rate. A curve whose slope is 2x at every point is an antiderivative of 2x.

cases.label: Slope of the total at minute 2

steps.headline: Subtracting the totals at the two ends

lead.text: The running total gives a quick way to find the water that arrives in the middle of a run. Suppose you want the water that flows in between minute 2 and minute 3. By minute 3 the total is A(3) = 9 litres, and 4 of those had already arrived by minute 2. What is left is 9 − 4 = 5 litres.

The picture confirms it. Between minutes 2 and 3 the region under the line is a strip 1 minute wide, with heights 4 and 6 at its sides. Its area is the average height, 5, times the width, 1, which is 5 litres. The subtraction and the geometry agree.

afterFigure.text: In general, the area under a rate from a to b is the running total at b minus the running total at a, and the running total is an antiderivative F of the rate.
This is the fundamental theorem of calculus. To find an area under a rate you find an antiderivative, put in the two ends and subtract. No rectangles or triangles are needed.

lead.text: Here is the whole method on a rate with two terms.

steps.headline: Find the integral of 4x + 3 from 1 to 2.

workedSteps.text: Undo the rate one term at a time.
Put in the top end and the bottom end.

steps.headline: Find the integral of 2x + 1 from 0 to 2.

workedSteps.text: Undo each term of the rate.
Put in the ends and subtract.

lead.text: One loose end remains. Earlier in the course a rate turned out to have a whole family of antiderivatives, F(x) + C, one for every constant C. That leaves a choice about which of them goes into the subtraction.

Take F(x) = x² and G(x) = x² + 4, and use both on the tap's rate between minute 1 and minute 3. With F the total is 9 − 1 = 8 litres. With G it is (9 + 4) − (1 + 4) = 13 − 5 = 8 litres. The 4 is added at the top end and taken away again at the bottom end, so it leaves no trace.

The same happens for any constant. Using F + C gives (F(b) + C) − (F(a) + C), and the two Cs cancel to leave F(b) − F(a). That is why a definite integral is a single number even though its antiderivative is a whole family, and why you may take C = 0 and leave the constant out.
Think about what happens to a constant that is added to F when you put in the top end and then the bottom end.

reveal.text: The same constant was added to F(b) and to F(a), so subtracting one from the other removed it.

steps.headline: How fast the running total grows

lead.text: Back to the running total, now for any rate f. Let A(x) be the amount that has built up from a fixed starting time up to x. It is the area under f between the start and x, and it is called an accumulation function.

As x increases, the right-hand end of the area moves. Push it a tiny step to the right and the area gains a thin sliver. The sliver is almost a rectangle as wide as the step and as tall as the rate at that moment, f(x). So the gain per unit of step is f(x), which says that the accumulation grows at the rate f(x) at its moving end.

afterFigure.text: For the tap, f(t) = 2t and A(x) = x². At minute 3 the bath is gaining water at 6 litres per minute, which is the height of the rate graph there and also the slope of the running total. Integrating a rate and then differentiating the result bring you back to the rate. The two operations undo each other, and this is the second half of the fundamental theorem.

cases.label: Slope of the total at minute 3

lead.text: A running total grows at the rate at its moving end. Use that for a different rate.

reveal.text: You put x = 4 into the rate itself. The total built up so far is a different number, and its growth rate at that moment is the rate f(4).

lead.text: A(x) is the integral of t² + 1 from 0 to x. You do not need to integrate it. Ask how fast A is growing.

reveal.text: A′(x) was the rate itself, evaluated at the moving end. Integrating and differentiating undo each other.

lesson.orientation: Evaluate definite integrals with antiderivatives and differentiate accumulation functions.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Run a bath with a tap that you open a little wider every minute. After t minutes the water arrives at 2t litres per minute, so the flow starts from nothing and keeps climbing. You want to know how much water has gone in after three minutes, and there are two ways to find out.

The first is the one you have just been practising: draw the flow against time and measure the area under the line. The second comes from earlier in the course. Take the flow rate, work backwards to a formula it could have come from, and read the amount off that formula. Each of them turns a rate into an amount, and until now they have looked like two separate tools.

This lesson puts them side by side on the same bath. They agree, and the reason they agree is one of the main results of calculus. Once you see it, finding an area under a rate graph no longer needs rectangles or triangles. It needs a subtraction.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out a definite integral by subtracting an antiderivative's values, and say how fast an accumulated amount is growing.
intro.whyItMatters: It replaces slow area counting with one subtraction.

recap.keyIdea: The integral of f from a to b is F(b) − F(a), where F′ = f, and the amount accumulated grows at exactly the rate f.

blocks.text: You counted the tap's first two minutes as a triangle and got 4 litres, and the first three as 9. The running total x² gave the same 9 as its value at 3 minus its value at 0. For 4x + 3 on [1, 2] you found 9, and for 2x + 1 on [0, 2] you found 6. For a running total of the rate 3t, the growth at x = 4 was 12.

recap.nextHook: You can now turn a rate into an amount by undoing it and subtracting. The next lesson uses that on tanks that fill and leak and on a car that turns round, where the units and the starting amount matter.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the integral of 2x from 1 to 3.
hints: Use an antiderivative and subtract its value at the lower bound.
The squared function is an antiderivative of the given linear rate.
Subtract its lower-endpoint value from its upper-endpoint value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: An antiderivative is x²; endpoint subtraction gives 9 − 1 = 8.

misconceptions.feedback: 9 is the antiderivative at the top only. Subtract its value at the bottom.
6 is the rate at x = 3. Use the antiderivative at the ends.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the integral of 2x + 1 from 0 to 2.
hints: Integrate each term before applying the bounds.
An antiderivative contains a squared term and a linear term.
Evaluate that antiderivative at both bounds and subtract in upper-minus-lower order.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: An antiderivative is x² + x, giving (4 + 2) − 0 = 6.

misconceptions.feedback: Integrate each term: the 1 gives an x as well.
5 is the rate at x = 2. Use the antiderivative at the ends.

questions.prompt: Why does the arbitrary constant disappear when a definite integral is evaluated using F(b) − F(a)?
hints: Both endpoints use the same antiderivative.

acceptedIdeas: The same constant is subtracted from itself
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Using F + C gives F(b) + C − F(a) − C, so the constants cancel.

choices.label: The same constant is subtracted from itself

questions.onCorrect: The same constant is added to F(b) and F(a), so it cancels.

misconceptions.feedback: Antiderivatives differ by constants, and any of them works. That is why the constant has to cancel.
Constants do have values. They cancel in the subtraction.

questions.prompt: Let A(x) be the integral from 0 to x of (t² + 1) dt. Find A′(2).
hints: The derivative of accumulation is the current rate.
The moving upper bound is the input of the original integrand.
Evaluate that integrand at the requested boundary.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The fundamental theorem gives A′(x) = x² + 1, so A′(2) = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. A′(x) is the integrand at the moving bound: 2² + 1.

misconceptions.feedback: Include the +1: evaluate the whole integrand.
2 is the bound. Put it into the integrand.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the integral of 3x² from 1 to 2.
hints: Evaluate the antiderivative at both endpoints.
The given quadratic's antiderivative is a cubic.
Evaluate the cubic at both bounds and subtract.

misconceptions.feedback: 8 is the antiderivative at the top only. Subtract its value at the bottom.
12 is the rate at x = 2. Use the antiderivative at the ends.

questions.prompt: Which procedure correctly evaluates a continuous rate's definite integral?
hints: The graph being accumulated and the antiderivative play different roles.

acceptedIdeas: Subtract endpoint values of an antiderivative
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The theorem uses F(b) − F(a), where F′ = f.

choices.label: Subtract endpoint values of an antiderivative
Find area under the antiderivative instead

questions.onCorrect: Subtract the antiderivative's values at the ends: F(b) − F(a).

misconceptions.feedback: The antiderivative gives totals, not areas under itself. Subtract its end values.
Derivatives of the ends are rates. The integral needs totals.

questions.prompt: A tap's flow rate after x minutes is r(x) = 2x litres per minute. What is the area under the graph of r from x = 0 to x = 3?
hints: What shape is the region under a straight line from 0?
The base is 3. How tall is the line at x = 3?
Half of base times height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The region is a triangle with base 3 and height 2 × 3 = 6, so its area is ½ × 3 × 6 = 9.

questions.onCorrect: 9. A triangle is half of base times height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is base × height. A triangle is half of that.
6 is the height at x = 3. The area needs the base too.

hints: F(b) counts everything up to b. What does F(a) count?

acceptedIdeas: It is the total at b minus the total at a
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: F(b) is the total built up to b and F(a) is the total built up to a. The difference is what was added from a to b.

choices.label: It is the total at b minus the total at a
Because a is smaller than b

questions.onCorrect: F(b) − F(a) is what accumulates between a and b: the total at the end minus the total at the start.

misconceptions.feedback: The result can be negative. The subtraction removes what built up before a.
The order is set by what accumulates, not by which number is smaller.

questions.prompt: A pool gains water at r(t) = 6t litres per minute. How many litres does it gain between t = 1 and t = 3 minutes?
hints: Which function has derivative 6t?
3t² does. Find its value at t = 3 and t = 1.
Subtract the value at 1 from the value at 3.
questions.onCorrect: 24. Undo the rate, then subtract the totals at the ends.

misconceptions.feedback: 27 is the total at t = 3 only. Subtract the total at t = 1.
18 is the rate at t = 3. The question asks for an amount.

questions.prompt: F(x) = 2x² has derivative 4x. Use it to find the integral of 4x from 0 to 3.
hints: Which function do you evaluate at the ends?
Put 3 and 0 into 2x².
Top minus bottom.
questions.onCorrect: 18. The antiderivative at the top minus the antiderivative at the bottom.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 is the rate at x = 3. You need the antiderivative's values at the ends.

questions.prompt: A(x) is the amount accumulated from 0 to x at rate f(t) = 3t. How fast is A growing at x = 4?
hints: How fast does an accumulation grow at a moment?
At the current rate, f.
Put 4 into f.
questions.onCorrect: 12. The accumulation grows at exactly the current rate.

misconceptions.feedback: 24 is the amount accumulated, A(4). The question asks how fast it is growing.
3 is the coefficient in the rate. Put x = 4 into the rate itself.

Choosing F(x) = x² + 4 gives the same endpoint difference as x²; the arbitrary constant cancels when subtracting.
Any antiderivative gives the same endpoint difference, because the constant is added at both ends and cancels.
For continuous f, A(x) = ∫ from a to x of f(t) dt has derivative A′(x) = f(x).
If A accumulates the rate f(t) = 3t, then A′(4) = f(4) = 12.
The instantaneous growth rate of the accumulation is the height of the original rate function at the moving boundary.
An antiderivative is x² + x, giving (4 + 2) − 0 = 6.
Using F + C gives F(b) + C − F(a) − C, so the constants cancel.
The fundamental theorem gives A′(x) = x² + 1, so A′(2) = 5.

The region is a triangle with base 3 and height 2 × 3 = 6, so its area is ½ × 3 × 6 = 9.
